notes:
Now let me compile all the notes. I have extensive content from Enduring Word (David Guzik), Precept Austin (with Spurgeon, Ryle, Robertson, MacArthur quotes), Gill's Exposition, and Ellicott's Commentary. I also have John Piper (Desiring God, Reformed Baptist). Here are the verse-by-verse notes:

---

## Matthew 2 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — After Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea, during the time of King Herod, Magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem

- **"After Jesus was born"** — Matthew gives little detail of the birth itself (that is in Luke 2); his focus is on what happened *after*. The word "after" suggests a gap of months, perhaps up to two years (see v. 16). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- **Bethlehem** means "house of bread" — fitting for the birthplace of the One who called Himself the Bread of Life (John 6:35). It was David's ancestral home, a small town about six miles south of Jerusalem. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary) ; [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- **"In the days of Herod the king"** — This is Herod the Great, an Idumean (Edomite) appointed by Rome. Ellicott notes that his death occurred in 4 BC, meaning Jesus was born sometime in 5 or 4 BC — our calendar is several years off. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- Herod was a brilliant builder (including the Temple) but monstrously cruel. He murdered his wife Mariamne, her mother, and at least three of his own sons. Emperor Augustus reportedly quipped it was safer to be Herod's pig (*hus*) than Herod's son (*huios*). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- **"Magi from the east"** — The Greek word is *magoi*, referring to a priestly caste from Persia/Media skilled in astronomy, astrology, and dream interpretation. They were not kings (that tradition traces to Tertullian, c. AD 225, influenced by Psalm 72:10–11 and Isaiah 60:1–6). The tradition of three Magi comes only from the three gifts; their names (Melchior, Caspar, Balthasar) are medieval legends. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm) ; [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- Gill argues at length that the Magi came from Persia, not Chaldea (which is north, not east, of Judea) or Arabia. He also argues they arrived close to two years after the birth — otherwise Herod would not have targeted boys up to two years old. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/2.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/2.htm)
- A. T. Robertson: Matthew's purpose is to "show the reception given by the world to the new-born Messianic King. Homage from afar, hostility at home; foreshadowing the new faith: reception by the Gentiles, rejection by the Jews." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary)
- Spurgeon: "When Jesus was born, there came wise men from the east. There is infinite power even in an infant Savior." Also: "The shepherds did not miss their way; they came to Christ at once, while the wise men, even with a star to guide them, yet missed their way, and went to Jerusalem instead of to Bethlehem." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon](https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon)

### v. 2 — asking, "Where is the One who has been born King of the Jews? We saw His star in the east and have come to worship Him."

- **"Born King of the Jews"** — Remarkable phrasing: a baby is *born* a king, not merely destined to become one later. "His kingly status was not conferred on him later on; it was from birth" (Carson, cited in Guzik). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- **"His star in the east"** — Ellicott says this means they saw it while *they* were in the east, not that the star was in the eastern sky. Gill notes the star was "a new and an unusual one," appearing specifically to signal the birth. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/2.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/2.htm) ; [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- **What was the star?** Guzik surveys proposals: a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn, a supernova, a comet, or a uniquely created supernatural phenomenon. Spurgeon believed it was "a luminous appearance in mid-air; probably akin to that which led the children of Israel through the wilderness." John Piper similarly stresses it was supernatural: "it is doing something it cannot do on its own: guiding magi to the Son of God." [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/we-have-come-to-worship-him](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/we-have-come-to-worship-him) ; [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- The Magi likely knew Numbers 24:17 ("a Star shall come out of Jacob") — an ancient Jewish text widely regarded as Messianic. Gill also discusses a tradition that Zoroaster (founder of the Magian sect) himself predicted a star would announce a great king. Ellicott adds that both Tacitus and Suetonius record a widespread Eastern expectation that a world ruler would arise from Judea. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/2.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/2.htm) ; [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- **"Come to worship Him"** — Spurgeon emphatically rejects Unitarian interpretations that this was mere civil homage to a human king: "The magi believed that he who was born King of the Jews was more than a human being, and they had come to worship him." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon](https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon)

### v. 3 — When King Herod heard this, he was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him.

- Herod was pathologically paranoid about rivals. Having already killed multiple family members, the news of a "born King of the Jews" threatened his rule. Ellicott notes that at this time Herod was near death, his son Antipater was under condemnation, and his last days were consumed by "frenzied and cruel suspicion." [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- **"All Jerusalem with him"** — Two possible reasons (Guzik): (a) the people rightly feared Herod's paranoid, violent reaction; or (b) the size and dignity of the Magi's caravan caused general alarm. Gill suggests they feared "tumults, commotions and wars" might erupt. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/) ; [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/2.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/2.htm)
- Spurgeon: "It is an ill sign of a man's heart when that which is for the good of all men becomes a trouble to him. It is an ill stomach that turns good meat to poison." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon](https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon)

### v. 4 — And when he had assembled all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where the Christ was to be born.

- **"Chief priests"** likely included former High Priests (Herod changed the office frequently) and heads of the 24 priestly courses. **"Scribes"** (*grammateis*) were the professional interpreters of the Law, mostly Pharisees. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/) ; [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- Ellicott says this was probably not a formal Sanhedrin meeting but "a Committee of Notables" called for this specific purpose. Herod "acts as if he himself shared their Messianic hopes" to gauge their thinking. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- Guzik notes a tragic irony: this was the religious leaders' first contact with Jesus. They knew the Bible's answer perfectly — but showed no personal interest in going to meet the Messiah themselves. "They understood the Biblical information correctly, but failed in application to their lives." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- Spurgeon: "When the earth-king dabbles in theology, it bodes no good to truth. Herod among the priests and scribes is Herod still." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon](https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon)

### v. 5–6 — "In Bethlehem in Judea," they replied, "for this is what the prophet has written: 'But you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah…'"

- The quotation is from **Micah 5:2**, freely paraphrased. The Hebrew reads "you are little among the thousands of Judah"; Matthew's version (as quoted by the scribes) says "by no means least." Ellicott explains: "The prophet contrasts the outward insignificance with the spiritual greatness. The paraphrast sees the outward transfigured by the glory of the spiritual." [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- It distinguished "Bethlehem of Judea" from another Bethlehem in Zebulun (Joshua 19:15). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- The scribes quoted the promise of the **Ruler who will shepherd** God's people — a striking image of the Messiah as both King and Shepherd. Ellicott notes, however, that they stopped short of Micah's next words about the Ruler "whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting" — perhaps not wanting to raise the issue of the Messiah's deity before Herod. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- Guzik: "Sadly, these experts had the right information but seem personally uninterested in meeting the Messiah for themselves." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)

### v. 7 — Then Herod called the Magi secretly and learned from them the exact time the star had appeared.

- "Secretly" — Herod did not want others to know his true purpose. Ellicott notes Herod was probably himself a believer in astrology and "haunted by fears of what the star portended." [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- **"The exact time the star had appeared"** — Literally "the time of the appearing star." This detail becomes critical later: it establishes the age range of the children Herod would slaughter (two years and under, v. 16). Guzik: "We can assume that the wise men first saw the star a year or so previously (on the night Jesus was born)." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)

### v. 8 — And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: "Go and search carefully for the Child, and when you find Him, report to me, so that I too may go and worship Him."

- Bethlehem was only about six miles from Jerusalem. Ellicott: "So far as the mission became known, it would impress the people with the belief that he too shared their hopes." [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- The irony is heavy: Herod claimed he wanted to worship but intended murder. Spurgeon: "Mark that the wise men never promised to return to Herod; they probably guessed that all this eager zeal was not quite so pure as it seemed to be, and their silence did not mean consent." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon](https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon)

### v. 9 — After they had heard the king, they went on their way, and the star they had seen in the east went ahead of them until it stood over the place where the Child was.

- The star apparently **reappeared** after the Jerusalem visit and now moved to guide them specifically. Guzik: "This was an obviously supernatural phenomenon." France (cited by Guzik): "The words *came to rest* mean literally 'came and stood', and can mean only that the star itself moved to guide the Magi." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- Ellicott suggests they started toward Bethlehem in the evening, and as they went, saw the star shining in that direction. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- Adam Clarke proposed that the phrase "stood over where the young Child was" literally meant it stood *over the head of the child* — a meteor-like phenomenon that may have given rise to the halo in Christian art. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)

### v. 10 — When they saw the star, they rejoiced with great delight.

- John Piper notes the Greek piles up words for joy: "they rejoiced exceedingly with great joy" — a quadruple expression. "True worship is not just ascribing authority and dignity to Christ; it is doing this joyfully." [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/we-have-come-to-worship-him](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/we-have-come-to-worship-him)
- The star had apparently been absent during their time in Jerusalem (they had to ask directions). Its reappearance caused overwhelming joy. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)

### v. 11 — On coming to the house, they saw the Child with His mother Mary, and they fell down and worshiped Him. Then they opened their treasures and presented Him with gifts of gold and frankincense and myrrh.

- **"The house"** — By this time, Joseph and Mary were no longer in the stable/manger of Luke 2. The census crowds had dispersed; they had found lodging. Jesus is called a "young Child" (*paidion*), probably 6–18 months old. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/) ; [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- **"Fell down and worshiped Him"** — The Child is mentioned before Mary (against custom). Joseph is notably absent — perhaps at work. Trapp (cited by Guzik): "Joseph haply was at work, or otherwise absent, lest the wise men should mistake him for the true father of the child." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- **The three gifts**: Guzik notes the traditional symbolic reading: **gold** = royalty, **frankincense** = divinity (burned in worship), **myrrh** = death (used in embalming). However, Ellicott cautions that "the patristic interpretation of the gifts as significant … cannot be assumed to have been definitely present to the mind of the Evangelist." The Magi probably simply brought the finest gifts suitable for a king. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm) ; [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- Piper identifies four elements of true worship from this verse: (1) ascribing authority to Christ ("King of the Jews"), (2) ascribing dignity (falling down), (3) doing so with joy (v. 10), and (4) with sacrificial gifts. [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/we-have-come-to-worship-him](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/we-have-come-to-worship-him)
- Spurgeon: "Those who look for Jesus will see him: those who truly see him will worship him: those who worship him will consecrate their substance to him." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon](https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon)
- Meyer (cited by Guzik): the gold was providential — it funded the family's flight to Egypt and stay there. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)

### v. 12 — And having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they withdrew to their country by another route.

- Ellicott suggests they retired to Bethlehem's inn after worship, and were warned in their sleep. They likely crossed the Jordan fords rather than returning through Jerusalem. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- Obedience is as much a part of worship as gifts and bowing. Guzik: "Their worship is also manifested in obedience." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- Ellicott notes that Christendom has rightly seen the Magi as "the first-fruits of the outlying heathen world, the earnest of the future ingathering." The Feast of Epiphany (January 6) celebrates the "Manifestation of Christ to the Gentiles." [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)

### v. 13 — When the Magi had gone, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream. "Get up!" he said. "Take the Child and His mother and flee to Egypt. Stay there until I tell you, for Herod is going to search for the Child to kill Him."

- Note the careful phrasing: "the Child and His mother" — not "your wife and child." Ellicott calls this "significantly reverential." The Child always takes precedence. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- Egypt was a natural refuge: it was a well-ordered Roman province outside Herod's jurisdiction, and Philo records about a million Jews lived there. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- The command is urgent — the angel appears as soon as the Magi depart. Guzik: "It doesn't speak well of humanity to notice that when God added humanity to His deity and came to earth … the almost immediate reaction of one section of humanity was to try as hard as they could to murder Him." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)

### v. 14 — So he got up, took the Child and His mother by night, and withdrew to Egypt

- Joseph's obedience was immediate — the very night of the dream. Guzik: "Joseph's rapid and complete obedience is impressive." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- Spurgeon: "Night journeys, both actual and spiritual, may fall to the lot of those who carry Jesus with them." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon](https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon)
- Ellicott adds that the brevity of the narrative is itself "an argument for the non-mythical character of the narrative." Later apocryphal gospels added fabulous details (idols bowing, a spring appearing, robbers attacking and being saved by the future penitent thief). Matthew records none of that. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)

### v. 15 — where he stayed until the death of Herod. This fulfilled what the Lord had spoken through the prophet: "Out of Egypt I called My Son."

- The quotation is **Hosea 11:1**, which in its original context referred to Israel's exodus from Egypt. Matthew sees Jesus as the true and greater Israel — the Son of God recapitulating Israel's history. Ellicott: "In the days of the Exodus, Israel was the one representative instance of the Fatherhood of God … Now there was a higher representative in the person of the only begotten Son." [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- Guzik: "Matthew makes it clear that even as Israel as a nation came out from Egypt, so would the Son of God." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- The stay in Egypt was likely only a few months, since Herod died soon after (spring of 4 BC). [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)

### v. 16 — When Herod saw that he had been outwitted by the Magi, he was filled with rage. Sending orders, he put to death all the boys in Bethlehem and its vicinity who were two years old and under, according to the time he had learned from the Magi.

- **"Outwitted"** — literally "mocked" or "trifled with." Herod's rage was consistent with his known character. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- **The massacre**: Ellicott estimates Bethlehem's population at about 2,000, meaning the number of murdered boys was probably **between 20 and 30**. This small number explains why Josephus (the main source for Herod's life) did not record it — it was a local atrocity easily overlooked amid Herod's many grand-scale crimes. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- Guzik: "Though there are no exact descriptions of this event in secular history, it is entirely in character with Herod's well-known ruthlessness." In his final days, Herod ordered the execution of leading men of Judea so there would be genuine mourning at his own funeral. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- The age range "two years old and under" confirms the Magi arrived well after the birth night. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary)

### v. 17–18 — Then what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled: "A voice is heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more."

- From **Jeremiah 31:15**. In its original context, Rachel (the symbolic mother of Israel) weeps as her descendants are led into Babylonian exile from Ramah (Jeremiah 40:1 — the staging point where captives were sorted for death or exile). [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- **Rachel's tomb** was near Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19), about one mile north — making the imagery natural for Matthew. The sorrow of the Babylonian exile is recapitulated in the sorrow of Bethlehem's mothers. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- Matthew sees a pattern: just as exile preceded restoration in Jeremiah's day, so the sorrow of the innocents precedes the salvation brought by the Child who escaped. Jeremiah 31 is ultimately a chapter of hope — the very next verses promise Israel's restoration. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)

### v. 19–20 — After Herod died, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt. "Get up!" he said. "Take the Child and His mother and go to the land of Israel, for those seeking the Child's life are now dead."

- Herod died in 4 BC, shortly before Passover, of a painful and loathsome disease (described graphically by Josephus). The angel's message echoes Exodus 4:19, where the Lord tells Moses in Midian, "all those who wanted to kill you are dead." Jesus is being patterned after both Israel and Moses. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- The plural "those … are dead" is notable: Herod alone was named, but others may have been involved in the plot, or the angel deliberately echoes the Exodus phrasing. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/) ; [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)

### v. 21 — So Joseph got up, took the Child and His mother, and went to the land of Israel.

- Guzik: "We also notice Joseph's quick obedience." Four times in this chapter Joseph receives divine direction through dreams, and each time he obeys immediately. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)

### v. 22 — But when he learned that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. And having been warned in a dream, he withdrew to the district of Galilee

- **Archelaus** was one of Herod's sons, who inherited Judea, Samaria, and Idumea under Herod's final will. He was never officially recognized as "king" (only ethnarch), but Matthew uses the popular term. He was so brutal and incompetent that in AD 6 the Romans deposed him at the Jews' request and replaced him with a Roman governor. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm) ; [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- Joseph's fear was well-founded. Archelaus began his reign by slaughtering 3,000 Passover pilgrims. A dream warning confirmed Joseph's natural caution and redirected the family to Galilee, ruled by the milder Herod Antipas. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)

### v. 23 — and he went and lived in a town called Nazareth. So was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophets: "He will be called a Nazarene."

- **Nazareth** was an obscure, unmentioned-in-the-Old-Testament village in Galilee. It had a poor reputation — "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" (John 1:46). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- **"He will be called a Nazarene"** — There is **no single Old Testament verse** that says this. Guzik explains that Matthew is summarizing a **theme** from multiple prophets: the Messiah would be despised and humble. The word "Nazarene" (possibly related to the Hebrew *netzer*, "branch," Isaiah 11:1) evokes both the Messianic "Branch" prophecies and the contempt associated with Nazareth. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- Note the plural: "spoken through the **prophets**" — not "the prophet." Matthew signals that he is not quoting a single text but gathering a prophetic theme. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/)
- Spurgeon sees deep meaning in the obscurity: the Son of God grows up in a despised town, foreshadowing His rejection by the very people He came to save. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon](https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon)

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

Given the limits of the sources accessed, denominational distinctives on this chapter are less pronounced than on doctrinal passages. However, several points of emphasis emerge:

- **Reformed / Ligonier / Desiring God**: Strong emphasis on the *sovereignty of God* in orchestrating all events — the star, the Magi's journey, the dreams, the flight to Egypt — to fulfill prophecy and bring the nations to worship Christ. John Piper: "God wields the universe to make his Son known and worshiped. This is his great goal in all things." [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/we-have-come-to-worship-him](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/we-have-come-to-worship-him)
- **Baptist / Spurgeon**: Emphasis on personal conversion and the three responses to Jesus (hatred, indifference, worship) as representing all humanity. Spurgeon also stresses that the wise men's worship was directed to Christ's deity, not mere kingly homage — a direct rebuttal of Unitarian readings. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon](https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary-spurgeon)
- **Wesleyan / Ryle** (cited by Precept Austin): Emphasis on the *cost of discipleship* — the Magi's "spiritual diligence" and the trouble they undertook to find Christ. "Where is our self-denial? What pains do we take about our souls? What does our religion cost us?" [https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-2-commentary)

(Note: Distinctive Lutheran, Pentecostal, and Methodist commentaries on this chapter were not accessible within the search limits of this session. The sources available — Guzik/Calvary Chapel, Spurgeon/Baptist, Piper/Reformed Baptist, Ellicott/Anglican, Gill/Baptist — are broadly representative of conservative evangelical and Reformed Protestant readings.)

## Other Views (Limited by Available Sources)

- **Catholic tradition**: Though specific Catholic commentary pages could not be fetched in this session, the sources note that the tradition of the Magi as **three kings** named Gaspar, Melchior, and Balthasar can be traced to Tertullian (c. AD 225) and was perpetuated by Christian art and medieval legend. Their supposed skulls are venerated at Cologne Cathedral. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-2/) ; [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/2.htm)
- **Modern scholarship / NET Bible**: Ellicott notes that some modern critics treat the Magi narrative as "purely mythical," but that this view "with hardly an exception" extends skepticism to every supernatural element in the Gospels — a broader debate, not a finding specific to this chapter. He argues there are "no special notes of a legendary character" that distinguish this narrative from the rest of Matthew.
